etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mintar-a-. Cognate with Okinawan 乱りゆん (njariyun).
Compare みだら (midara, “obscene, indecent”), 乱(みだ)す (midasu, “to disturb”), and 乱(みだ)りに (midari ni, “haphazardly, randomly”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 再(さい) (sai-, “re-, again”) + 生(せい) (sei, “live, life”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 区切(くぎ)る (kugiru)..

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From かた (kata, “hard; solid”, root of かたい) + める (-meru, “-ify”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 崖 (MC ngje|ngea, “cliff, precipice”). Not attested in isolation. First attested in compound 崖岸 (gaigan, “cliff shore, cliff bank”) in 900.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Shift from older pronunciation kake. First attested in 1280.
May be a shift in usage from compounding element kake as in the synonymous terms 懸路 (kakeji), 懸道 (kakemichi, “cliff road, steep mountain road”), where the kake comes from verb 懸ける (kakeru, “to set into; to set across”), from the way the road would be set into the cliff or mountain.
The change from kake to gake apparently happened some time during the Edo period (1603–1868). This term is recorded as Caqe (then-current Portuguese orthography for modern romanization kake) in the 1603 Nippo Jisho Japanese-Portuguese dictionary.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Further derivation unclear.
First attested in the Man'yōshū of 759.
Modern references either omit this reading entirely or provide no pitch accent information for this reading, suggesting that it might be archaic or even obsolete in modern usage.

etymologies.heading: Etymology

Derivation unclear. First attested in the late 1100s.
Modern references either omit this reading entirely or provide no pitch accent information for this reading, suggesting that it might be archaic or even obsolete in modern usage.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Probably from 岸 (kishi, “shore, bank (of a body of water)”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. In modern Japanese, only found as a prefix in compounds. Possibly contracted from 弓 (yumi, “bow”), as most derived terms exhibit voicing of the second component.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *yumi. Appears in the Man'yōshū (c. 759 CE), with a phonetic spelling of 由美 ⟨yumi₁⟩, */yumʲi/.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Alteration from torashi, 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb torasu, from tora as the 未然形 (mizenkei, “incomplete form”) of verb 取る (toru, “to take”) + す (su, honorific suffix in Old Japanese). Original meaning was “something kept to hand”.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 弓 (MC kjuwng). Compare modern Mandarin 弓 (gōng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology

etymologies.heading: Etymology

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Coined by Japanese medical scientist Okuyama Torafumi in 1872 in his work 医語類聚 (Igo ruiju) as a translation of English affection.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 敏感 (min^X + kom^X).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with Japanese 解く (hodoku).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Originally a compound of 木(こ) (ko-, the 被(ひ)覆(ふく)形(けい) (hifukukei, “bound form”) of 木(き) (ki, “tree”)) + 末(すえ) (sue, “tip, end”).
The sue changes to zue as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 正(せい) (sei, “correct, right”) + 解(かい) (kai, “solution, explanation, understanding, answer”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Probably from Middle Chinese compound 貧弱 (MC bin nyak, literally “poor + weak”). Compare modern Mandarin 貧弱／贫弱 (pínruò, “poor and weak”).
Alternatively, may have been coined in Japan of Middle Chinese-derived elements 貧 (hin, “poor”) + 弱 (jaku, “weak”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Regular shift in conjugation from Classical Japanese verb 重んず (omonzu), a phonetic shift from Classical Japanese 重みす (omomi su), from 重 (omo, stem of adjective 重い (omoi, “heavy”)) + み (-mi) + す (su, “to do”), where みす (-mi su) was a grammaticalised pattern meaning “treat (noun) as (adjective); find (noun) (adjective)”. Literally, “to treat as heavy”. Compare the kango (漢語) 重視 (jūshi, “value, esteem, respect”), from 重 (“heavy; important”) + 視 (“to see”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Perhaps related to Goguryeo 乃勿 (*namur). Compare Korean 납 (nap).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 鉛 (MC ywen).
